lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: What you said the other day to Odysseus about death, Achilles—it was beneath you. Unworthy of both your teachers, Chiron and Phoenix. I was listening when you told him you’d rather be a field-hand working for some landless peasant than be king of all the dead. Now, some cowardly Phrygian might say that—someone clinging to life far past the point of decency. But for the son of Peleus, the most fearless hero of them all, to think so little of himself? It’s an embarrassment. It makes a mockery of everything you did in life. You had the choice. You could have stayed in Phthia and lived a long, obscure life as a king, but you willingly chose to die for glory.

lines.speaker: Achilles
lines.text: Son of Nestor... back then I had no experience of this place. I didn't know which was better. I threw away my life for that wretched little scrap of glory. Now I understand that it is useless, no matter how many epics the living sing about it. Down here, everyone has the exact same status. The beauty is gone, Antilochus. The strength is gone. We all lie in the exact same darkness, indistinguishable from one another. The dead Trojans don't flinch when they see me. The dead Greeks don't salute me. There is absolute equality. A dead man is a dead man, coward or hero. [sighs] It eats at me. It breaks my heart that I am not alive, even as a slave.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: Even so, what can anyone do, Achilles? Nature has decreed that absolutely everyone must die. We have to abide by the law and stop torturing ourselves over the inevitable. Besides, look at how many of your friends are right here with you. Odysseus will be along soon enough. There’s comfort in company, in knowing you're not the only one. Look at Heracles, and Meleager, and the other great men. I don't think they would accept an offer to go back up, even if someone offered to let them be serfs for destitute peasants.

lines.speaker: Achilles
lines.text: Spoken like a true friend. But somehow, just the memory of life is a torment. I know it is for all of you, too. And if you won't admit it, you're only worse off, suffering in silence.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: No, we're better off, Achilles. Because we see that talking about it does no good. We've chosen to stay quiet, bear it, and endure—so we don't make fools of ourselves, the way you do, wishing for things like that.
